title: Curation
html:
The world is like an infinite garden of information where each data point is like a flower — some smell like springtime, while others reek of dead animals; some deserve our attention, while others are better ignored. Each day, we struggle to decide which flowers to pick and which to pass by, for it is with these flowers that we decorate the walls of our mind.

Do we pick the pretty ones? The loud ones? The sad ones? The compassionate ones? The hateful ones? The thoughtful ones? The anxiety-inducing ones? The enriching ones? The unifying ones?

Our walls are finite, but the garden is infinite. So we can’t pick all of the flowers, nor should we. We must curate. Will we cover our walls with darkness, levity, or a delicate balance of the two? We’ll spend our whole lives between these walls, so it makes sense to be thoughtful with how we select the decor.

Inevitably, our walls will have dark spots. Life will have its way with us. But apart from the unavoidable pains of being human, most of the information — the flowers — we pay attention to is done so voluntarily. We can choose which part of the world to focus on. We can decide how to decorate.

But focusing our attention during the Internet age is a strange thing. The aperture through which we view the world is so narrow, and its scope so limited, that, if we so choose, we can curate the information we see so that it is nearly uniform: entirely positive, entirely negative, entirely about cats, or dogs, or skateboarders taking nut shots. The Internet, if used with intentionality, enables us to set up information filters and tune our social media algorithms so we only see what we want to, nut shots and all. We can bias our information intake to include only that which makes our days brighter and our relationships stronger. This is an incredible feature! However, if used thoughtlessly, the Internet will feed us only that which keeps us hungry. And we already know how that story ends. We see it everywhere:

Everyone wants to be right. Nobody wants to be together.

So, my recommendation is simple. Unless your livelihood depends on staying up to date on the latest news on a given topic, I believe it’s counterproductive to try. Adopt a low-information (or more like low-news) diet. After all, most of us don’t want to be informed. We want to feel informed. And these are not the same thing. Being informed requires deep study, a practice with which 99.9% of people yelling at each other on the Internet are not well-acquainted.

Additionally, attending too much to the Bad will make the world seem much grimmer than it is, and it will keep us from enjoying the miraculous ocean of wonders in which we swim every day. We’ll become like the young fish in the story told by David Foster Wallace during a commencement speech, completely oblivious to the obvious and ever-present context in which they live:

“ These two young fish are swimming along and they happen to meet an older fish swimming the other way, who nods at them and says ‘Morning, boys. How’s the water?’ And the two young fish swim on for a bit, and then eventually one of them looks over at the other and goes ‘What the hell is water?’ ”

What we pay attention to matters, for what we pay attention to determines the quality of our minds, and the quality of our minds determines the quality of our lives.

*deep exhale*

It’s snowing as I’m writing this.

It has been all day.

I went to a coffee shop earlier to escape my studio apartment.

When I walked outside, the icy storm greeted me.

It greeted me warmly.

I paid attention to what was around me.

I noticed the shimmer of the snowflakes dancing against the backdrop of streetlights.

It felt like a “Hello.”

It made me smile.

I put that flower up on my wall.
